newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Irish islands vote, leaders brush up for TV debate.
newsitem.headline: Irish islands vote, leaders brush up for TV debate.

text.p: About 200 people on tiny Irish islands cast their votes two days early on Wednesday while Prime Minister John Bruton and his challenger, Bertie Ahern, rehearsed their lines for a televised election debate.

People on the islands of Clare, Inishturk and Inishbiggle were forced to vote early to make sure that balloting is not disrupted by any bad weather when the rest of Ireland's two million voters go to the polls on Friday.

The three islands are off the west Mayo coast and can only be reached by sea. Seventeen other Irish islands are voting on Friday because they are accessible either by helicopter, small airplane or high-speed ferry.

Some islanders voting on Wednesday complained that they were being robbed of a final opportunity to make up their minds when Bruton and Ahern clash in the final television debate of a three-week campaign on Wednesday night.

"It is entirely unsatisfactory as the last two days of the campaign are vitally important to voters," said Donal O'Shea, a community development office on Clare, which has a population of 137 according to government figures.
A leading political analyst said that there were increasing signs from opinion polls that the result of the election, which should be known on Sunday, would be inconclusive.
Professor Michael Laver of Trinity College said neither of the two competing coalitions looked likely to get the 83 seats needed for a majority, and the televised debate could be crucial.

He said neither the centre-right opposition of Fianna Fail and the Progressive Democrats nor the government's centre-left alliance of Fine Gael, Labour and Democratic Left would emerge clear winners on Sunday.
"It looks even more likely there will be a hung Dail (parliament) now," he told Irish Radio.
Laver said this put pressure on Fianna Fail's Ahern and Bruton, the leader of Fine Gael, to "really go for it tonight" when the two hold the only televised head-to-head debate of the campaign.
"The stakes are pretty high now because the result looks too close," Laver said.
The prospect of a hung parliament worries Irish financial markets which fear that a long period of horse-trading between blocs competing to form a coalition could disrupt economic policy.

Irish Finance Minister Ruairi Quinn of the Labour Party quickly quashed speculation of a politically unpopular interest rate rise to choke inflation and defend the Irish pound, which hit a six-year low against sterling on Tuesday.
"I do not believe there is any need whatsoever for an interest rate increase," he told Irish radio. "Fears of inflation...would not in my view materialise."
The ruling coalition is campaigning on a platform of sustained economic growth and prosperity since it took over when the previous Fianna Fail-led government collapsed at the end of 1994.
But opinion polls have consistently shown Fianna Fail and its Progressive Democrats ally ahead of the government since campaigning started.

Laver said the two coalitions might need the support of small parties such as the Greens to form a government or that the Labour Party, despite protests to the contrary, might go back into government with Fianna Fail if the result is close.
Fianna Fail moved on Tuesday night to crush speculation of a rift with the Progressive Democrats, who have been calling for 25,000 job reductions in the civil service.
The two parties issued a statement saying there would be no compulsory redundancies in the civil service at all.
